title: Laparoscopic repair of perforated duodenal ulcer
subtitle: Omental patch, washout, treat the cause

sources.title: Perforated and bleeding peptic ulcer: WSES guidelines
The management of intra-abdominal infections from a global perspective: 2017 WSES guidelines

indications: Perforated duodenal or juxtapyloric ulcer with peritonitis confirmed on CT or erect chest radiograph, in a patient fit for pneumoperitoneum.
Laparoscopy is preferred by WSES where the expertise exists and the patient is haemodynamically stable.
contraindications: Haemodynamic instability or septic shock not responding to resuscitation: open repair is faster and more controlled.
A large perforation (commonly cited as above about 2 cm), a perforation with bleeding, or suspected gastric outlet obstruction: these need an open and often more extensive operation.
Non-operative management can be considered only in a carefully selected stable patient with a sealed perforation on contrast imaging, under close senior surveillance. It is the exception.
preparation: Resuscitate, nasogastric decompression, urinary catheter, intravenous proton pump inhibitor.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics per local protocol for intra-abdominal infection; add antifungal cover only for specific risk groups as locally advised.
Ask about non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, steroids, smoking and previous ulcer disease; plan Helicobacter pylori testing.
Consent to include conversion to open, leak from the repair, intra-abdominal collection, and the possibility that a gastric perforation is malignant.
positioning: Supine, French position (legs apart) or American, with reverse Trendelenburg for the upper abdomen and Trendelenburg later for pelvic washout.
Strap the patient securely; the table will tilt in several directions.
equipment: 30-degree laparoscope, three to four ports, liver retractor if needed.
Atraumatic graspers, needle holders, 2/0 or 3/0 absorbable sutures on a curved needle.
Suction-irrigation and several litres of warm saline.
Nasogastric tube in place for air or dye testing.
anatomy: Most perforated duodenal ulcers are anterior, on the first part of the duodenum just distal to the pylorus. The pyloric vein (of Mayo) marks the pylorus.
A posterior duodenal ulcer bleeds into the gastroduodenal artery rather than perforating. A perforation with haematemesis suggests kissing ulcers.
The greater omentum hangs from the greater curve and usually provides a well-vascularised pedicle that reaches the duodenum without tension.
The common bile duct lies behind the first part of the duodenum. Deep sutures at the inferior edge of the perforation risk it.
criticalSafety: Biopsy any gastric perforation, because a perforated gastric cancer can look exactly like a benign ulcer.
Do not attempt to close a friable perforation primarily under tension. The omentum seals the hole; the sutures only hold the omentum.
Convert to open early for instability, poor view, a large perforation or difficult tissue. Conversion is a safety decision.
Treat the cause after the operation: Helicobacter pylori eradication and stopping non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs prevent recurrence.
structuresAtRisk: Pylorus, which can be narrowed by over-zealous sutures
Transverse colon and its mesentery when mobilising the omentum
commonErrors: Tying the sutures over the perforation first and strangulating the friable edges.
An omental patch under tension that pulls off.
Incomplete washout, leaving collections in the subphrenic spaces and pelvis.
Omitting a biopsy of a gastric perforation.
complications: Leak from the repair, presenting with ongoing sepsis and peritonitis.
Gastric outlet narrowing from a bulky repair.
Wound and port-site infection, chest infection, and the systemic complications of peritonitis.
Recurrent ulceration if Helicobacter pylori or drug causes are not addressed.
postop: Nasogastric decompression only as long as clinically needed; feed early once there is no sign of leak.
Continue proton pump inhibitor; test for and treat Helicobacter pylori.
A short, defined course of antibiotics after adequate source control, as WSES advises, extended only for ongoing infection.
Stop non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; review the need for steroids, antiplatelets and anticoagulants.
Endoscopy at follow-up after a gastric perforation to confirm healing and obtain histology.

steps.emphasis: Therapeutic antibiotics for peritonitis should already be running.
French position with secure strapping: reverse Trendelenburg for the repair, head-down for the pelvic washout.
Open (Hasson) entry is safer in a distended septic abdomen.
Find the perforation by following the fibrin and bile to the anterior duodenum. If it is gastric, it needs a biopsy.
Air via the nasogastric tube with the repair under saline, or dilute methylene blue.
Laparoscopic washout of all four quadrants, subphrenic spaces and pelvis with warm saline until the return is clear.
A drain near the repair is optional; WSES does not mandate one.
Biopsy only for a gastric perforation. Duodenal ulcers are not routinely biopsied.
Hand over the Helicobacter pylori test, the drug review and any biopsy result to chase.

step.pdu.expose.title: Exposing and assessing the perforation
step.pdu.expose.why: The size, site and tissue quality of the perforation decide whether a laparoscopic patch is the right operation. That decision is made in the first five minutes, not after an hour of struggling.
how: Lift the liver edge to expose the pylorus and first part of the duodenum.
Aspirate contaminated fluid around the perforation and send a sample for culture.
Measure the perforation against an instrument jaw and assess the edges: friable, indurated or healthy.
Locate the omentum and check that a pedicle will reach the defect without tension.
pitfalls: Starting the repair before deciding whether this perforation suits a laparoscopic patch.

step.pdu.patch.title: Omental patch repair
step.pdu.patch.why: A perforated ulcer edge is inflamed and holds sutures poorly. A vascularised omental plug seals the hole; the sutures exist only to hold the omentum in place. Tying them over the hole first strangulates the edges and enlarges the defect.
how: Place three interrupted absorbable sutures across the perforation, taking full-thickness bites of healthy duodenum well back from the edge, oriented along the long axis so the pylorus is not narrowed.
Bring a tongue of well-vascularised omentum over the perforation and lay it under the sutures.
Tie the sutures gently over the omentum, enough to hold it, not to throttle it.
Alternatively, for a small perforation with healthy edges, primary closure reinforced with omentum is acceptable.
pitfalls: Tying the sutures to close the hole before laying the omentum.
A thin, pale strip of omentum that devascularises.

step.pdu.convert.title: When to convert or change the operation
step.pdu.convert.why: Laparoscopy is a means to a good repair and a thorough washout, not an end. Most failed laparoscopic repairs are ones in which the warning signs were visible early.
how: Convert to open for haemodynamic deterioration, poor view, an inability to wash out adequately, or tissue that will not hold a patch.
A large perforation may need a jejunal serosal patch, a pyloric exclusion, a resection, or a controlled duodenostomy: these are senior and often open decisions.
A perforation that is bleeding as well needs the gastroduodenal artery controlled, which usually means an open duodenotomy.
Call for senior help before, not after, the repair has failed.
pitfalls: Persisting laparoscopically because conversion feels like failure.
